lines: In 2007, Katherine Kinzler and her team at Harvard found that people start to prefer their own group when they are babies.
They did a study with five-month-old babies whose families only spoke English.
In one, a woman spoke English, and in the other, a woman spoke Spanish.
Then both women appeared on the screen without speaking.
At that point, the babies paid more attention to and looked longer at the English speaker.
This showed that the babies were more interested in the English speaker.
In another study, babies were also more likely to take a toy from someone who spoke their language.
These results suggest that we naturally like people who are similar to us.
body.text: In 2007, Katherine Kinzler and her team at Harvard found that people start to prefer their own group when they are babies. They did a study with five-month-old babies whose families only spoke English. The babies watched two videos. In one, a woman spoke English, and in the other, a woman spoke Spanish. Then both women appeared on the screen without speaking. At that point, the babies paid more attention to and looked longer at the English speaker. This showed that the babies were more interested in the English speaker. In another study, babies were also more likely to take a toy from someone who spoke their language. These results suggest that we naturally like people who are similar to us.
